chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad al-Hannat, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed and for him were a mother, a father, and a son. So the son said, 'I want to kill my father's killer.' And the father said, 'I forgive.' And the mother said, 'I want to take the wergild.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So let the son give the mother of the killed one one-sixth of the wergild, and give to the inheritors of the killer one-sixth of the wergild as the right of the father who forgave, and let him kill him.'

key_terms.أَعْفُو: I forgive (waive the right to kill)

ai.seo_question: How is qisas divided when the mother, father, and son of the deceased have different wishes regarding the killer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of prioritizing the son's right to qisas (retaliation) even when the father has already forgiven the killer, resolving the conflict between the mother's claim to diyah and the son's claim to execution. The ruling allocates one-sixth of the wergild to the mother and another sixth to the father's heirs, reflecting the specific shares of guardianship in Shia inheritance and blood-money jurisprudence. It highlights the nuance where forgiveness by one guardian does not extinguish the right of another, provided the latter chooses retaliation.
